blocks.text: 29.12 Drum Buss
blocks.raw_html: 29.12 Drum Buss

blocks.text: Drum Buss is an analog-style drum processor that was designed to add body and character to a group of drums, while gluing them together in a tight mix.

blocks.text: 29.13 Dynamic Tube
blocks.raw_html: 29.13 Dynamic Tube

blocks.text: The Dynamic Tube effect infuses sounds with the peculiarities of tube saturation. An integrated envelope follower generates dynamic tonal variations related to the level of the input signal.

blocks.text: Three tube models, A, B and C, provide a range of distortion characteristics known from real amplifier tubes. Tube C is a very poor tube amp that produces distortions all the time. The qualities of Tube B lie somewhere between these two extremes.

blocks.text: 29.17 Erosion
blocks.raw_html: 29.17 Erosion

blocks.text: Erosion adds digital degradation to the input signal by modulating a short delay using a combination of a sine wave and filtered noise. It can produce a range of effects, from noisy artifacts to downsampling-like distortions.
blocks.raw_html: Erosion adds digital degradation to the input signal by modulating a short delay using a combination of a sine wave and filtered noise. It can produce a range of effects, from noisy artifacts to downsampling-like distortions.

blocks.text: The frequency spectrum of the input signal is shown in the display during playback, along with a visual representation of the modulation. The display also functions as an X-Y controller, which you can use to adjust the Freq and Amount controls. Click and drag along the X-axis to change the sine wave frequency and the center frequency of the noise filter. Drag along the Y-axis to control the modulation amount. You can hold Alt (Win) / Option (Mac) to adjust the filter width of the noise modulation on the Y-axis instead. Note that the filter width has no effect when using only sinusoidal modulation.

blocks.text: 29.30 Redux
blocks.raw_html: 29.30 Redux

blocks.text: The Redux effect has a variety of parameters for creating a wide range of jagged and edgy sounds. You can radically mangle any source material, with effects ranging from harsh distortion and digital aliasing artifacts to warm, fat 8-bit grit. Extra noise and stereo width can be added to the downsampling process, while filtering further transforms the sound. The quantizer’s amplitude curve can also be changed to allow both subtle and drastic bitcrushing.

blocks.text: 29.30.2 Bit Reduction
blocks.raw_html: 29.30.2 Bit Reduction

blocks.text: The bit reduction controls are available on the right side of the device. Bit reduction decreases the number of bits used to represent the digital signal, reducing dynamic range while adding distortion and noise. At extreme settings, all original dynamics are lost and sounds are reduced to jagged square waves.

blocks.text: 29.33 Roar
blocks.raw_html: 29.33 Roar

blocks.text: Roar is a saturation and coloration device with up to three processing stages and a range of flexible routing configurations. Its selection of non-linear shaper curves and filters can be combined to produce a wide variety of saturation types, from targeted warmth to sweeping harmonic motion or glitchy blasts of noise. Roar’s feedback controls and built-in compressor add a further layer of distinctive possibility to the device, which can produce sounds unlike any other instrument or effect currently available in Live.

blocks.text: The Drive knob sets the level of the signal being input into Roar before the gain stages. It can be used to quickly add or remove distortion without having to adjust individual Shaper Amount controls across multiple gain stages, for example, or to modify an input signal to ensure a preset behaves as expected.

blocks.text: The Tone Amount knob changes the input signal’s balance of high and low frequencies. When set to positive values, high frequencies are boosted and low frequencies are attenuated. When set to negative values, low frequencies are boosted and high frequencies are attenuated.

blocks.text: Adjusting Roar’s Tone parameters has noticeable effects on the timbre of its gain stages, as these follow the Input section in Roar’s processing chain. blocks.text: The Serial routing mode processes the input signal using two concatenated shapers. The Blend control blends between the sound of Stage 1 and the sound of Stages 1 and 2 combined.

This mode serves a variety of applications, including drum processing and adding saturation to entire mixes.

The delayed signal is sent to the second stage without being scaled by the feedback gain, which produces single (distorted) repetitions or slapbacks. blocks.text: The Feedback section is one of Roar’s most distinctive features. Feeding Roar’s signal back into itself can add a new layer of ringing, otherworldly tones and textures to your sound.

blocks.text: 29.34 Saturator
blocks.raw_html: 29.34 Saturator

blocks.text: Saturator is a waveshaping effect that can add that missing dirt, punch or warmth to your sound. It works by applying non-linear shaping to the input signal, with results ranging from soft saturation to intense coloration.
blocks.raw_html: Saturator is a waveshaping effect that can add that missing dirt, punch or warmth to your sound. It works by applying non-linear shaping to the input signal, with results ranging from soft saturation to intense coloration.

blocks.text: Saturator shapes the incoming signal by mapping each individual value in the signal to a new value according to a selected shaping curve. Because this is usually a non-linear process, the incoming signal is dynamically reshaped based on its level at each moment in time.

blocks.text: You can select the curve used for shaping the input signal from the Curve Type chooser. There are eight types to choose from: Analog Clip, Soft Sine, Bass Shaper, Medium Curve, Hard Curve, Sinoid Fold, Digital Clip, and Waveshaper.

blocks.text: The available curve types offer various shaping characteristics. Digital Clip applies immediate, hard clipping when exceeding the clipping point, while Analog Clip introduces a smoother transition around the clipping point. These curves remain linear for signal levels below the clipping point. The Soft Sine, Medium Curve, and Hard Curve types apply saturation with different sonic characteristic. Sinoid Fold is a wavefolding type — as the input signal gets louder, the output folds over itself, producing unusual textures.

blocks.text: The Bass Shaper curve is somewhat similar to Analog Clip, but presents a smoother harmonic spectrum when driving low frequency signals with high gain. This makes it ideal for processing low-end signals like 808 kick drums and synth basslines.

blocks.text: Bass Shaper includes an additional Bass Shaper Threshold control, which sets the threshold for the curve from 0 to -50 dB. The curve remains linear when the input signal is below the threshold but smoothly starts to clip once the signal exceeds the threshold. This allows you to move continuously from one form of clipping to another: low threshold values produce soft clipping and high threshold values produce hard clipping. Low threshold values work best for bass signals, especially when combined with high Drive values.

blocks.text: 29.41 Vinyl Distortion
blocks.raw_html: 29.41 Vinyl Distortion

blocks.text: The Vinyl Distortion effect emulates some of the typical distortions that occur on vinyl records during playback. These distortions are caused by the geometric relationships between the needle and the recorded groove. The effect also features a crackle generator for adding noisy artifacts.
blocks.raw_html: The Vinyl Distortion effect emulates some of the typical distortions that occur on vinyl records during playback. These distortions are caused by the geometric relationships between the needle and the recorded groove. The effect also features a crackle generator for adding noisy artifacts.

blocks.text: The Tracing Model section adds even harmonic distortion to the input signal. Adjust the amount of distortion with the Drive knob, or click and drag vertically in the Tracing Model X-Y display. To adjust the distortion’s frequency or ”color,” drag horizontally in the X-Y display or double-click on the Freq field and type in a value. Holding the Alt (Win) / Option (Mac) modifier while dragging vertically in the X-Y display changes the frequency band’s Q (bandwidth).

The Hi-Quality mode reduces aliasing and improves sound quality (especially with high frequency signals), at the cost of a slight increase in CPU usage. The Pre-DC Filter mode activates a DC filter at Saturator’s input stage, which is useful for removing DC offsets from audio that contains them.

The Vinyl Distortion effect emulates some of the typical distortions that occur on vinyl records during playback. These distortions are caused by the geometric relationships between the needle and the recorded groove. The effect also features a crackle generator for adding noisy artifacts.

quotes.quote: Sets created prior to 12.4 that include Erosion will load the previous version of the device, which is now named Erosion Legacy.

The Redux effect has a variety of parameters for creating a wide range of jagged and edgy sounds. You can radically mangle any source material, with effects ranging from harsh distortion and digital aliasing artifacts to warm, fat 8-bit grit. Extra noise and stereo width can be added to the downsampling process, while filtering further transforms the sound. The quantizer’s amplitude curve can also be changed to allow both subtle and drastic bitcrushing.

Once MIDI sidechain is enabled, use the External Source chooser under MIDI From to specify the MIDI sidechain source. You can also choose whether the signal should be received Pre FX or Post FX via the Tapping Point chooser.

source_questions.question: WET postclip bounds do not bound an arbitrary added dry mixture; inverted/mirrored Color EQ is not exact cancellation. No unconditional independent Post Clip disable inferred.

quotes.quote: You can select a post-clipping stage for all the curve types using the Post Clip Mode chooser below the Shaper Curve display. When Soft Clip or Hard Clip is selected, Saturator’s output will never exceed the level set by the Output control. This is particularly useful for controlling any additional boost created by negative Color values.

The Color toggle enables the device’s two color filters, which produce a color curve visualized in the device’s expanded view. The color filters adjust an EQ curve that is first applied before the shaper, then applied again, inverted, after the shaper. This allows you to, for example, remove bass frequencies before the shaper, so that only mid/high frequencies are saturated and the energy of the bass is maintained in the output.

The Output control attenuates the signal level of Saturator’s final output. When Soft Clip is activated in the Post Clip Mode chooser, Saturator will also apply an instance of the Analog Clip curve to the device’s output.
The Dry/Wet control sets the balance between dry and processed signals in Saturator’s output. Set it to 100% when using Saturator in a return track.

source_questions.question: Zero envelope removes follower modulation only, Waveshaper Drive 0 scopes its path only, and zero input proves neither noise absence nor tail completion. No finite-trial infinity/RNG claims.

quotes.quote: Attack and Release are envelope characteristics that define how quickly the envelope reacts to volume changes in the input signal. Together, they shape the dynamic nature of the distortions. Note that if Envelope is set to zero, they will have no effect.

When the Feedback Gate toggle is turned on, Roar’s feedback automatically fades out when an input signal is no longer being sent into the device. When turned off, Roar’s feedback continues indefinitely.
Drive determines how much the Waveshaper curve’s parameters affect the input signal. At 0%, these parameters have no effect on the Waveshaper curve. At 100%, these parameters fully shape the curve.
The Crackle section adds noise to the signal, with noise density set by the Density control. The Volume control adjusts the amount of gain applied to the noise.

Aliasing can be reduced by enabling Hi-Quality mode, which can be accessed via the device title bar’s context menu. This improves the sound quality, particularly with high frequency signals, but there is a slight increase in CPU usage.

S & H (Sample and Hold) generates a random constant value that changes to a new random value at an interval determined by the Noise Rate. This is useful for creating stepped random modulation patterns in Roar’s output signal.
